SASCOC Olympics

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Is South Africa ready for the Olympics?

Unique Selling Point:
Exclusive interview with Barry Hendricks, the newly elected President of SASCOC.
A look at SASCOC's submission to Parliament on their plans for the Tokyo Olympics in July 2021.
An interview with one of the SASCOC Five, a group of committee members who claim that Barry Hendrick's election was improperly tabled.
Interviews with some of the athletes who have qualified and hope to compete at the Olympics.

Summary:
Barry Hendricks was elected as South African Sports Confederation and Olympic Committee (SASCOC) President, with many – especially athletes hoping this will be the beginning of the end of years of turmoil at the sporting mother body. This follows years of infighting and boardroom squabbles, capped off by Gideon Sam standing down as President in 2019 when he reached the age limit of 70. SASCOC had initially been due to hold its Presidential election on March 28, before the Annual General Meeting was postponed due to the coronavirus pandemic, and Barry Hendricks was elected in September 2020, when the AGM sat. The process was a series of disputes, including a claim that, when Acting President, Hendricks had blocked the candidacy of rivals prior to the election and was unethical. Hendricks denied the allegation but was placed on special leave amid an investigation. The sporting officials, dubbed the "SASCOC Five" – which included, Skhosa Kobus Marais, Cecilia Molokwane, Jerry Segwaba and Kaya Majeke, had lodged a claim which alleged that the motion to clear Hendricks had been included on an unauthorised agenda, provided by Sam Ramsamy.

So what do we know about Barry Hendricks … well Hendricks has a long-time involvement
in sport and represented Eastern Province in tennis, squash, judo and athletics. He was also involved in the National Sports Council, driving the Protea Muso Programme. He was chairman of Squash SA and is an active member in the senior and masters squash leagues for Jeppe Club. He was also the President of the Gauteng Sports Council. Off the field of play he’s an accredited facilitator and has served as team manager and volunteer coordinator for SA at some major internationals. Hendrick has promised to work for athletes.


Further information:
The cash-strapped body had also been plagued by controversies under the previous executive‚ with senior managers being fired amid claims of corruption and sexual harassment and a ministerial committee of inquiry probing corporate governance issues in 2018, Hendricks has promised accountability!
Who suffers? Last year SASCOC tabled a plan to parliament where they envisaged that they would get a haul of 13 medals at the Tokyo Olympics… In truth where will the medals come from? For years athletes have had to fund most of their sporting activities…because of lack of funding and support from SASCOC and sub-bodies. The South African hockey team is busy fundraising for the Olympics, after being told there is not enough money to go around. Both the men’s and women’s Olympic team are in limbo despite qualifying for the Olympics. This is just the tip of the iceberg, some of our Olympians will be required to pay their own way to the Olympics. But there is a glimmer of hope as former and currently Olympians are hoping to fight even harder for athletes, As new members of the Athletes Commission were elected recently The members include Godfrey Kgotso Mokoena, who won Olympic and world long jump silver medals in 2008 and 2009, respectively, and Bridgitte Hartley, bronze medallist in the K1 500 metres canoeing at the London 2012 Games. Ernst van Dyk, double Paralympic and world para-cycling champion, Sizwe Ndlovu, who won gold in the coxless fours rowing at the London 2012 Olympics, Jeff Coetzee, tennis doubles specialist and Davis Cup player, and Louzanne Coetzee, 2016 Paralympian and holder of the women’s 5,000m world record in the T11 visual impairment category, have also been elected. It remains to be seen if Barry Hendricks will work well with these members who represent the athletes or will this all implode before or after the Olympics.

Press Release:


An Olympic Feat – SASCOC’s Road to Tokyo

Starved of international competition due to the pandemic, the world’s athletes are in the final stretch of preparing for the Summer Olympic Games. Tokyo 2020 was postponed to July 2021 and the world is holding its breath to see if the Games will proceed despite a resurgence of COVID-19 and slow vaccination rates. Carte Blanche sits down with Barry Hendricks, newly-elected President of the South African Sports Confederation and Olympic Committee (SASCOC), for a look at how SASCOC is dealing with a legacy of corruption, financial mismanagement and allegations of sexual abuse. We also preview the medal hopefuls who are now counting the days before they fly out to Japan.

Producer: Kate Barry | Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli

Script:


SASCOC OLYMPICS

V/O: Tokyo – the largest megacity in the world – and host of the biggest sporting event on Earth, the Olympic Games. Postponed because of the global pandemic - Tokyo 2020 will kick off in July - and South Africa will be there.

Rassie: If you can represent South Africa at the highest peak of any sportsman at the Olympic games, it’s a huge honour.

Tyson: I mean it’s not just your country, it’s also your continent as a whole that you to be representing. It’s Africa and the whole. So we’ve got a lot of responsibility on our shoulders, but at the same time it’s the biggest accolade in our sporting code and yeah, it’s a huge honour to play for your country as well.

V/O: These young hockey players echo the hopes and aspirations of every South African who’s ever competed at the Olympic Games. And with every medal won the country celebrated their triumph and a star was born. At Rio 2016 we achieved a record 10 medals – but while the athletes became legends, SASCOC was mired in controversy.

David: There's been a lot financial mismanagement. And the CEO and the CFO got fired for what appear to be very serious charges, although they are contesting that at the CCMA. I think one of the biggest things that hurts us was the infighting within the board, within the board. It's basically paralyzed them.

V/O: Veteran sports journalist David Isaacson reported on SASCOC’s woes for the Sunday Times - from the dismissal of former CEO Tubby Reddy to the 2018 findings and recommendations of the Inquiry led by the late Judge Ralph Zulman.

David: It was just like a hot mess that really has only been hopefully sorted out at last year's elections.

Link: SASCOC has often been in the news for all the wrong reasons, but now there’s a new Board and a new President. So what can we expect from the new team?

Barry: The membership of SASCOC have spoken. We as a board and we as the members of SASCOC voted this new board in and we are looking forward and moving forward.

V/O: Newly elected President Barry Hendricks represented Eastern Province in squash, tennis, judo and athletics.

Barry: I became an administrator of sport when I was about 17, 18 when I was asked to become the secretary of the tennis club in the coloured suburb of Port Elizabeth, called then Galvandale. When I was at Rhodes University with the black student movement I was the chairman of the tennis club. I then became an executive member of the Eastern Province Sports Council, then moved up as President of Squash in Africa, Gauteng Sports Federation and others. And because of that I have this affiliation with the needs of athletes, but also the needs of administrators.

Macfarlane: SASCOC has a deficit of R7 million. How will you deal with it?

Barry: We've already covered it. We don't owe any debt any longer. We are now working towards bringing in money for the Olympics, Paralympics, Africa Games. So we are now able to pay anyone that we owe. And now we're working on and building our coffers - through the IOC funding, through government funding, lottery funding.

Macfarlane: How many athletes are you taking to the Tokyo Olympics?

Barry: We are taking about 200 athletes for the Olympics and about 40 athletes for the Paralympics.

V/O: That’s the biggest team we’ve ever had, because in 2019 they voted to relax the selection criteria, and simply apply the IOC and IPC’s qualifying criteria.

Mac: Will SASCOC be taking all those athletes?

Barry: That’s the current policy, yes. If you qualify, you go.

Link: In the past just because you qualified for the Olympics, didn’t mean you would actually go. Some athletes had to raise money to fund their own participation. Will that be another hurdle for athletes this year?

Garreth: So we're not 100 percent sure yet about what our final Olympic costs are going to be, but all of our preparation, we have to cover those costs. And at the moment, if we're not careful, that comes out of the player's pockets.

V/O: Garreth Ewing is the coach of the South African Men’s Hockey Team. They have a crowdfunding initiative to cover their travel costs to competitions here and in Europe in preparation for Tokyo.

Mac: How much does each athlete need though, Garreth?

Garreth: We’ve been told to budget about 45K a person. But you know our operating costs between now and getting to Tokyo or getting back again from Tokyo, we’re looking at about three-and-a-half million.

Mac: And has SASCOC offered any help, any financial assistance for you guys to go?

Garreth: I know there's stuff going on behind the scenes, and I know that help is going to be offered. But we're just trying to control what we can control. And that's our preparation, which those costs are not going to be covered.

V/O: But Hendricks is confident that SASCOC will be able to get the funds necessary to pay for every athlete to go to the Olympics.

Mac: How much are you spending per athlete?

Barry: On average 35 000 per athlete, and that’s standard.

Mac: So what costs are covered by SASCOC and which are covered by the IOC?

Barry: The IOC gives us funding for all the accommodation and the costs of food at the Games. We have to cover flights, we have to cover the kits, we have to cover the medical expenses.

V/O: But Mr Price Sport has come to the party to sponsor the kit.

Barry: Mr Price and its own design team are creating a uniquely South African brand that will compete at the Olympics.

V/O: South Africans were mortified when our athletes turned out in the most embarrassing design disasters in London and Rio.

12:27 And so we’re not going to have that debacle that we had in Rio and..

Mac: The pyjamas of 2012 and 2016? Are you promising me Mr President?

Barry: No, I have full confidence in Mr Price.

V/O: Team SA may be getting free vellies for Tokyo, but SASCOC still needs an airline sponsor and funding for the medical team. Additional money is expected from government and the Lotto. But there’s another thorny issue which needs to be resolved before the Olympics.

Link: Sexual abuse has been a stain on South African sport for decades. Last year three swimming coaches were accused of abusing minors and the sports administrators came under fire for their handling of the allegations. So what is SASCOC doing to keep our athletes safe?

David: Swimming South Africa is at the coalface of those allegations. I think it's fair to say that at least in two of those three cases, the issues have not been handled properly.

Penny: Speaking across the board for all federations we need to make sure we have really strong policies in place and the procedures, but more importantly, that we then follow up and follow through with it. And I think a huge shift has to come in the mindset of sports administrators to ensure that the victim is the one that we look after.

V/O: Swimming icon Penny Heyns won the double gold medal in Atlanta in the one hundred and two hundred metre breaststroke in 1996 – an achievement that's never been equalled. She’s now involved in SportsVoice - offering a free safeguarding policy for sports clubs and federations worldwide.

Penny: We need education. If you look at the US system it’s mandatory for their coaches, for anybody on the national team to annually do this programme, and answer questions and go through it and get accredited on safeguarding.

Barry: We’ve adopted a safeguarding policy and we’ve entrenched the fact that each federation, national federation, must have a safeguarding policy.

V/O: SASCOC will also be taking action regarding Swimming SA ahead of the Tokyo Games.

Barry: There are new matters that have arisen and the current Safeguarding Commission have now forwarded even further recommendations to SASCOC as to how the Board must deal with that particular matter. And we will do it through the proper processes as well.

Link: South African athletes have been starved of international competition since the start of lockdown, but with the Olympic Games kicking off in July training is in full swing. So how many medals can we expect?

David: Tatjana Schoenmaker is a definite possibility for 2 medals.

V/O: The breaststroke champion broke two African records last week.

Penny: Tatjana, if she continues dropping times with the same kind of pace that she’s been doing up until now, then I think we can expect really big things from her.

David: I think Akani Simbine in the 100m he’s got a great chance, and I think the men’s 400m relay got a great chance. Wayde van Niekerk if he’s back. That’s another medal.

Sfx: I can’t believe it! He has obliterated Michael Johnson’s world record.

V/O: Surfing makes its Olympic debut in Tokyo and South Africa’s Jordy Smith is world number 4.

Barry: So for us, we want medals. But we also go to the Olympics to provide a platform and a stepping-stone for those youngsters who might not get medals this year but may get medals in Paris or the following year.

V/O: But with only 3 months to go until the Opening Ceremony more than 70% of Japanese polled want the Games delayed or cancelled. A resurgence of Covid infections means no foreign spectators will be allowed.

Barry: The IOC have also put on the table free vaccinations for every athlete in every country. They come first during these games and the support teams and the medical teams and the management teams are there to support them, to create a hassle-free environment for them to compete at their very best. So good luck to all the athletes. All the best.

Barry: I became an administrator of sport when I was about 17, 18 when I was asked to become the secretary of the tennis club in the coloured suburb of Port Elizabeth, called then Galvandale. When I was at Rhodes University with the black student movement I was the chairman of the tennis club. I then became an executive member of the Eastern Province Sports Council, then moved up as President of Squash in Africa, Gauteng Sports Federation and others. And because of that I have this affiliation with the needs of athletes, but also the needs of administrators. Macfarlane: SASCOC has a deficit of R7 million. How will you deal with it? Barry: We've already covered it. We don't owe any debt any longer. We are now working towards bringing in money for the Olympics, Paralympics, Africa Games. So we are now able to pay anyone that we owe. And now we're working on and building our coffers - through the IOC funding, through government funding, lottery funding. Macfarlane: How many athletes are you taking to the Tokyo Olympics? Barry: We are taking about 200 athletes for the Olympics and about 40 athletes for the Paralympics. V/O: That’s the biggest team we’ve ever had, because in 2019 they voted to relax the selection criteria, and simply apply the IOC and IPC’s qualifying criteria. Mac: Will SASCOC be taking all those athletes? Barry: That’s the current policy, yes. If you qualify, you go. Link: In the past just because you qualified for the Olympics, didn’t mean you would actually go. Some athletes had to raise money to fund their own participation. Will that be another hurdle for athletes this year? Garreth: So we're not 100 percent sure yet about what our final Olympic costs are going to be, but all of our preparation, we have to cover those costs. And at the moment, if we're not careful, that comes out of the player's pockets. V/O: Garreth Ewing is the coach of the South African Men’s Hockey Team. They have a crowdfunding initiative to cover their travel costs to competitions here and in Europe in preparation for Tokyo. Mac: How much does each athlete need though, Garreth? Garreth: We’ve been told to budget about 45K a person. But you know our operating costs between now and getting to Tokyo or getting back again from Tokyo, we’re looking at about three-and-a-half million. Mac: And has SASCOC offered any help, any financial assistance for you guys to go? Garreth: I know there's stuff going on behind the scenes, and I know that help is going to be offered. But we're just trying to control what we can control. And that's our preparation, which those costs are not going to be covered. V/O: But Hendricks is confident that SASCOC will be able to get the funds necessary to pay for every athlete to go to the Olympics. Mac: How much are you spending per athlete? Barry: On average 35 000 per athlete, and that’s standard. Mac: So what costs are covered by SASCOC and which are covered by the IOC? Barry: The IOC gives us funding for all the accommodation and the costs of food at the Games. We have to cover flights, we have to cover the kits, we have to cover the medical expenses. V/O: But Mr Price Sport has come to the party to sponsor the kit. Barry: Mr Price and its own design team are creating a uniquely South African brand that will compete at the Olympics. V/O: South Africans were mortified when our athletes turned out in the most embarrassing design disasters in London and Rio. 12:27 And so we’re not going to have that debacle that we had in Rio and.. Mac: The pyjamas of 2012 and 2016? Are you promising me Mr President? Barry: No, I have full confidence in Mr Price. V/O: Team SA may be getting free vellies for Tokyo, but SASCOC still needs an airline sponsor and funding for the medical team. Additional money is expected from government and the Lotto. But there’s another thorny issue which needs to be resolved before the Olympics. Link: Sexual abuse has been a stain on South African sport for decades. Last year three swimming coaches were accused of abusing minors and the sports administrators came under fire for their handling of the allegations. So what is SASCOC doing to keep our athletes safe? David: Swimming South Africa is at the coalface of those allegations. I think it's fair to say that at least in two of those three cases, the issues have not been handled properly. Penny: Speaking across the board for all federations we need to make sure we have really strong policies in place and the procedures, but more importantly, that we then follow up and follow through with it. And I think a huge shift has to come in the mindset of sports administrators to ensure that the victim is the one that we look after. V/O: Swimming icon Penny Heyns won the double gold medal in Atlanta in the one hundred and two hundred metre breaststroke in 1996 – an achievement that's never been equalled. She’s now involved in SportsVoice - offering a free safeguarding policy for sports clubs and federations worldwide. Penny: We need education. If you look at the US system it’s mandatory for their coaches, for anybody on the national team to annually do this programme, and answer questions and go through it and get accredited on safeguarding. Barry: We’ve adopted a safeguarding policy and we’ve entrenched the fact that each federation, national federation, must have a safeguarding policy. V/O: SASCOC will also be taking action regarding Swimming SA ahead of the Tokyo Games. Barry: There are new matters that have arisen and the current Safeguarding Commission have now forwarded even further recommendations to SASCOC as to how the Board must deal with that particular matter. And we will do it through the proper processes as well. Link: South African athletes have been starved of international competition since the start of lockdown, but with the Olympic Games kicking off in July training is in full swing. So how many medals can we expect? David: Tatjana Schoenmaker is a definite possibility for 2 medals. V/O: The breaststroke champion broke two African records last week. Penny: Tatjana, if she continues dropping times with the same kind of pace that she’s been doing up until now, then I think we can expect really big things from her. David: I think Akani Simbine in the 100m he’s got a great chance, and I think the men’s 400m relay got a great chance. Wayde van Niekerk if he’s back. That’s another medal. Sfx: I can’t believe it! He has obliterated Michael Johnson’s world record. V/O: Surfing makes its Olympic debut in Tokyo and South Africa’s Jordy Smith is world number 4. Barry: So for us, we want medals. But we also go to the Olympics to provide a platform and a stepping-stone for those youngsters who might not get medals this year but may get medals in Paris or the following year. V/O: But with only 3 months to go until the Opening Ceremony more than 70% of Japanese polled want the Games delayed or cancelled. A resurgence of Covid infections means no foreign spectators will be allowed. Barry: The IOC have also put on the table free vaccinations for every athlete in every country. They come first during these games and the support teams and the medical teams and the management teams are there to support them, to create a hassle-free environment for them to compete at their very best. So good luck to all the athletes. All the best. Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for SASCOC Olympics (5905) Kate Barry 22 April 2021

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Is South Africa ready for the Olympics?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Exclusive interview with Barry Hendricks, the newly elected President of SASCOC. A look at SASCOC's submission to Parliament on their plans for the Tokyo Olympics in July 2021. An interview with one of the SASCOC Five, a group of committee members who claim that Barry Hendrick's election was improperly tabled. Interviews with some of the athletes who have qualified and hope to compete at the Olympics.
metadata.Summary: Barry Hendricks was elected as South African Sports Confederation and Olympic Committee (SASCOC) President, with many – especially athletes hoping this will be the beginning of the end of years of turmoil at the sporting mother body. This follows years of infighting and boardroom squabbles, capped off by Gideon Sam standing down as President in 2019 when he reached the age limit of 70. SASCOC had initially been due to hold its Presidential election on March 28, before the Annual General Meeting was postponed due to the coronavirus pandemic, and Barry Hendricks was elected in September 2020, when the AGM sat. The process was a series of disputes, including a claim that, when Acting President, Hendricks had blocked the candidacy of rivals prior to the election and was unethical. Hendricks denied the allegation but was placed on special leave amid an investigation. The sporting officials, dubbed the "SASCOC Five" – which included, Skhosa Kobus Marais, Cecilia Molokwane, Jerry Segwaba and Kaya Majeke, had lodged a claim which alleged that the motion to clear Hendricks had been included on an unauthorised agenda, provided by Sam Ramsamy. So what do we know about Barry Hendricks … well Hendricks has a long-time involvement in sport and represented Eastern Province in tennis, squash, judo and athletics. He was also involved in the National Sports Council, driving the Protea Muso Programme. He was chairman of Squash SA and is an active member in the senior and masters squash leagues for Jeppe Club. He was also the President of the Gauteng Sports Council. Off the field of play he’s an accredited facilitator and has served as team manager and volunteer coordinator for SA at some major internationals. Hendrick has promised to work for athletes.
metadata.Further information: The cash-strapped body had also been plagued by controversies under the previous executive‚ with senior managers being fired amid claims of corruption and sexual harassment and a ministerial committee of inquiry probing corporate governance issues in 2018, Hendricks has promised accountability! Who suffers? Last year SASCOC tabled a plan to parliament where they envisaged that they would get a haul of 13 medals at the Tokyo Olympics… In truth where will the medals come from? For years athletes have had to fund most of their sporting activities…because of lack of funding and support from SASCOC and sub-bodies. The South African hockey team is busy fundraising for the Olympics, after being told there is not enough money to go around. Both the men’s and women’s Olympic team are in limbo despite qualifying for the Olympics. This is just the tip of the iceberg, some of our Olympians will be required to pay their own way to the Olympics. But there is a glimmer of hope as former and currently Olympians are hoping to fight even harder for athletes, As new members of the Athletes Commission were elected recently The members include Godfrey Kgotso Mokoena, who won Olympic and world long jump silver medals in 2008 and 2009, respectively, and Bridgitte Hartley, bronze medallist in the K1 500 metres canoeing at the London 2012 Games. Ernst van Dyk, double Paralympic and world para-cycling champion, Sizwe Ndlovu, who won gold in the coxless fours rowing at the London 2012 Olympics, Jeff Coetzee, tennis doubles specialist and Davis Cup player, and Louzanne Coetzee, 2016 Paralympian and holder of the women’s 5,000m world record in the T11 visual impairment category, have also been elected. It remains to be seen if Barry Hendricks will work well with these members who represent the athletes or will this all implode before or after the Olympics.
